payload.problem_addressed: Traditional CAD geometric kernels fit B-spline/NURBS surfaces using fixed heuristic initialization (predefined degrees, uniform knots, static control-point layouts) that ignores the procedural semantics and design intent encoded in modeling histories, producing suboptimal, semantically inconsistent fitting results.
payload.method_summary: LASP (Language-Augmented Semantic Priors) is a semantic reasoning layer above existing CAD geometric solvers: it translates a procedural modeling history (sequence of operations like Fillet, Shell, Chamfer) into rich-text semantic descriptions, then fine-tunes an LLM (Qwen3-14B) in a two-stage scheme (local operation-level prior learning, then global contextual prior learning over full histories) to autoregressively predict structured B-spline priors (degrees, control-point grid size, rationality, closure, trimming, continuity class, surface role) that bias the downstream solver's fitting/initialization toward semantically consistent surfaces, without modifying the solver itself.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper introduces LASP, described as the first language-driven framework that predicts structured B-spline priors from symbolic CAD modeling histories via rich-text semantic reasoning and a two-stage LLM fine-tuning pipeline. It shows these language-derived priors substantially improve both parameter-level prediction accuracy (e.g. B-spline detection F1 0.95 vs 0.51-0.67 for baselines) and, when instantiated as solver-accessible configuration choices, downstream engine-level fitting quality (71.2% RMS and 85.6% Hausdorff distance reduction), evaluated on an extended ABC-dataset subset via OpenCascade.
key_architecture_choices: Two-stage training: Stage I learns operation-only local geometric priors, Stage II extends to full modeling-history sequences with autoregressive dependencies across operations
Fine-tuned Qwen3-14B backbone (full-parameter fine-tuning) predicting structured JSON-like prior sequences via a single token-level NLL objective

Operates as an external semantic layer that does not modify the geometric kernel/solver internals; priors are injected as solver-accessible configuration choices (degree, closure, trimming) rather than inside the optimization loop
datasets: Extended subset of the ABC dataset (Koch et al. 2019), ~35,000 valid Stage I/II samples, ground-truth B-spline parameters derived from OpenCascade 7.8
metrics: Accuracy / Macro-F1 for degree, topology, rationality, continuity, role classification
payload.headline_results: LASP reaches F1=0.95 for B-spline detection (vs 0.51-0.67 baselines) and mean degree accuracy 0.85; at the engine level, semantically-guided fitting reduces RMS deviation by 71.2% and Hausdorff distance by 85.6% (p<0.001) versus default solver initialization.
claimed_advantages: Does not require modifying the geometric kernel/solver internals
Outperforms GPT-5 and DeepSeek-v3.2 baselines on continuity-class and surface-role prediction
Ablations show gains are not explainable by backbone scale alone -- semantic conditioning, Stage I geometric pretraining, and data augmentation each contribute
limitations: Semantic priors are not directly optimized inside the geometric kernel; they are only instantiated as discrete solver-accessible configuration choices rather than a full continuous injection into the fitting objective
Evaluation scope is limited to operations that produce B-spline surfaces (mainly Fillet, Chamfer, Shell) as covered by the ABC dataset
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: The core transferable mechanism is using an LLM/language-conditioned model to predict structured, solver-usable priors from a symbolic procedural history (construction-history-as-representation, our care area 3) that then bias a deterministic geometric solver's search -- directly analogous to using a learned model to propose structured parameters (e.g. block/sweep/projection command arguments) that steer hexgen's deterministic mesher toward valid, high-quality configurations. The two-stage local-then-global autoregressive prior prediction over a sequence of operations is also a reasonable template for conditioning program-token generation on accumulated context.
payload.reviewer_notes: This is not directly about hex-meshing or pointer/copy networks over B-rep graphs -- it targets B-spline surface fitting parameters, not mesh-generation programs, and its 'verifier' is a downstream fitting-error metric rather than a hard machine-checkable pass/fail gate. The LLM backbone (Qwen3-14B) is far larger than hexgen's 27M-parameter model, so the approach as implemented is not directly reusable at hexgen's scale; the transferable idea is the semantic-prior-as-solver-configuration-bias pattern, not the specific architecture.

provenance.method_summary: LASP does not modify the solver itself or introduce a new geometric optimization method; instead, it operates as a semantic reasoning layer above existing geometric kernels

provenance.claimed_advantages: LASP consistently outperforms all baselines, as shown in Table 1

payload.problem_addressed: The same CAD solid can be represented by many different, non-canonical B-reps (different face partitionings from different modeling operations, kernel re-export, rigid-motion placement, analytic-vs-NURBS surface encoding), and existing B-rep neural network encoders (UV-Net, BRepNet, AAGNet) are shown to be highly non-robust to this equivalence class, with performance collapsing catastrophically under such valid, meaning-preserving perturbations.
payload.method_summary: The paper introduces the canonical region graph: (1) canonical regions merge faces that are pieces of the same underlying analytic/NURBS surface into a single graph node, keyed by an exact surface identifier so merging is invariant to how the solid was originally partitioned into faces; (2) a canonical frame computed from the solid itself (centroid + principal axes of the boundary inertia tensor, with closed-form handling of sign and degenerate-eigenspace ambiguities) replaces the arbitrary file coordinate frame, and the solid is rescaled to unit boundary area for scale invariance. All 115 node / 10 edge features are computed as exact or mesh-quadrature integrals in this canonical frame, then passed through a standard 8-layer, 8-head edge-conditioned graph-transformer (17.5M parameters) with a linear per-region classification head. The paper proves (with proofs in the appendix) that the resulting graph and features are provably invariant to valid re-partitioning and rigid motions, and empirically verifies this on benchmark and real-world (Fusion 360, FreeCAD human-authored) B-reps.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper shows that popular B-rep encoders (UV-Net, AAGNet, BRepNet) are not robust to variation in B-rep partitioning, surface encoding, or rigid-body pose for the same underlying solid, with accuracy collapsing under standard-benchmark perturbations, kernel import/export round-trips, and a new human-authored FreeCAD dataset of designers modeling the same part differently. It proposes the canonical region graph, an input representation whose nodes/features/coordinate frame are derived from the solid itself, proves theoretical invariance guarantees to repartitioning and rigid motion, and shows it matches the strongest baseline on clean benchmarks while remaining stable under every tested perturbation, outperforming data augmentation as a fix.
key_architecture_choices: Canonical regions: faces merged into nodes via an exact deterministic surface key (analytic type+params, or NURBS control grid on the untrimmed underlying surface) plus shared-edge adjacency, so re-partitioning of the same surface does not change the graph

Canonical frame: origin at boundary centroid, axes at principal directions of the boundary inertia tensor, with closed-form sign-blending for near-degenerate skew and rotational-averaging for near-equal eigenvalues, constrained right-handed to preserve mirror distinctness
Scale normalization to unit total boundary area for scale invariance
115 node features / 10 edge features computed as exact integrals or mesh-quadrature-tolerant integrals (Lipschitz-bounded drift, Lemma 1) in the canonical frame
Standard graph transformer: 8 layers edge-conditioned multi-head attention, width 512, 8 heads, 17.5M parameters; face predictions inherit their region's prediction
datasets: Fusion 360 Gallery (3000 real parts, retrieval benchmark)
human-authored FreeCAD dataset (25 parts, 2 CAD experts)
CAD-Recode-based procedurally generated extrusion-partition dataset (1,049 pairs)
metrics: feature residual in units of training-set standard deviation (sigma)
payload.headline_results: Under automatic B-rep perturbations (repartitioning, NURBS re-expression, rigid motion) baseline encoders' mIoU collapses (e.g. AAGNet from 0.985 to as low as 0.006 under composed perturbations) while the canonical region graph stays flat at ~0.986-0.987 across all perturbations on MFInstSeg; predictive churn drops to ~0.00-0.02% versus 8.98-98.19% for baselines; on real Fusion 360 parts the method achieves 76-96% rank-1 self-retrieval versus 0.1-25.5% for the strongest baselines under most perturbations, and it beats all baselines even when they are trained with matching data augmentation.
claimed_advantages: Matches the strongest baseline's accuracy on standard clean benchmarks while being stable under every tested perturbation
Outperforms baselines trained with data-augmentation on the corresponding perturbation, without using any augmentation itself
Theoretical (proved) invariance guarantees to valid re-partitioning and rigid motion, not just empirical robustness
Verified via human study (independently-authored FreeCAD scripts of the same part) as well as automated perturbations and a real commercial-kernel (Rhino) import/export round-trip
limitations: Partition-invariance is a genuine cost when the discarded partition information is itself predictive: on Fusion 360 Gallery's per-operation-history labeling task the method underperforms B-rep-reading baselines on the clean dataset because it cannot exploit residual modeling-history traces in the partition
Mirror/degenerate-frame disambiguation is not guaranteed at ties: near-symmetric configurations (near-ties occur on 4.3% of MFInstSeg parts) degrade discrimination continuously rather than reliably

Only mesh-quadrature-computed features carry a Lipschitz stability bound (not exact invariance); only the exactly-integrated features (area, centroid, moments, type, axes/radii) are provably invariant
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: Highly applicable: hexgen's graph-transformer encoder reads a B-rep face/edge/vertex graph and hexgen explicitly has a closed 'rotation-invariant encoder' line -- this paper's canonical region graph offers a concrete, proven alternative/complementary mechanism (canonical frame from centroid + principal axes, scale normalization, exact-integral features) for rigid-motion invariance, plus a second axis of robustness hexgen does not appear to address: invariance to B-rep re-partitioning/re-triangulation artifacts, which is exactly the kind of domain-gap/tokenization-mismatch issue relevant when training on synthetic 'inverse factory' B-reps vs auto-labeled real CAD parts that may be partitioned differently by different kernels or construction templates. The face-merging-into-region-nodes idea could directly reduce spurious variation in hexgen's pointer/copy targets (addressing congruent/split faces) since multiple raw faces of one underlying surface collapse to one canonical node.
payload.reviewer_notes: Directly measures the same kind of representation robustness problem hexgen would face if trained on both synthetic inverse-factory B-reps and auto-labeled real CAD parts from different construction templates/kernels -- worth reading in full. Caveat: the method loses information that might correlate with 'how a part was built' (their Fusion-360 operation-labeling ablation), which is analogous to a concern for hexgen if any of its target programs are meant to reflect specific construction history rather than pure final-shape validity; also their pointer targets are per-region not per-original-face, which would require adapting hexgen's pointer/copy head to point at canonical regions instead of raw B-rep faces (or mapping region predictions back onto faces, as they do for segmentation).

provenance.method_summary: We propose the canonical region graph, an input representation whose nodes, features and coordinate frame are derived from the solid itself
